Makes it U.S. policy to promote the meaningful participation of women in conflict prevention, peace negotiations, and post-conflict recovery, and requires a government-wide strategy to carry that out.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 115-68](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/68){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 22 U.S.C. 2152j et seq.](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/2152j?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Required a national Women, Peace, and Security strategy, first issued in 2019, with agency implementation plans.
- Training for diplomatic, development, and defense personnel.
- Consultation with local women's groups and reporting to Congress.

## Why it matters

The United States was the first country to put the agenda of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1325 into a comprehensive statute. It is a companion to the [Global Fragility Act](gfa-2019.qmd) in the prevention and stabilization field.

## Current status

In force.

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}

- **Layer.** Specific authorization. Laws aimed at a particular conflict, country, program, or problem. Most work through a framework statute: an AUMF through the War Powers Resolution, a sanctions act through IEEPA. ([How the layers work](../study/index.qmd#the-authority-stack))
- **Codified in.** [Title 22 U.S.C.](title22-usc.qmd).
- **Era.** Sanctions, cyber, and great powers ([timeline](../study/timeline.qmd)).
- **Study.** [Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners](../study/units/assistance.qmd) (core reading); [Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations](../study/units/civilian-harm.qmd) (further reading).
